It is reported that the blessed body, when it leaves, the human soul is its sovereign — reward and punishment both belong to it — and its helpers and commanders and servants are all within the human being. The reward and punishment of the fingers specifically depends on what they hear, and whatever blood is shed comes from following it. The contented soul is the best of the three faculties of reason. The lower soul is beneath the rational soul, and the reproaching soul is its companion.

The common sense (hiss mushtarak) acts as the deputy and minister of the commanding soul (nafs ammara), and its anger is thus contained. The assembly of the chamberlain and the companion of the Shirvan is cunning and deceitful, and in its description it has been said: this sultan of passions, passions, and intrigues — the basest of souls endures patiently and presents its petition through desire, maintaining enmity with patience. The passions linger, and in the shared space between the commanding soul and the tranquil soul (nafs mutma'inna), those of the inner parts act as guardians. The outer and inner faculties are its soldiers, and they are powerful. The outer senses are: hearing, taste, touch, smell, and the inner faculties include the attractive faculty and imagination. The motive and cognitive faculties — these faculties are described by four attributes. Among these outer and inner faculties, the attractive power draws sustenance as it has been called, and it seeks daily provision. The retentive faculty serves like a servant, and the digestive faculty is its cook, and the taste faculty processes and separates, and the expelling faculty removes waste, and the smelling faculty acts as its scout. The seat of the brain is the master of the faculties; the memorizing faculty is the treasury-keeper of the kingdom; the imaginative faculty is its observer, perceiving both light and darkness; the hearing faculty serves as a spy in the corridor of the kingdom; and the informing faculty and the other mentioned faculties are the agents of the kingdom brought into existence. They travel as messengers in the realm, and whatever matters of benefit and harm, profit and loss, compatibility and incompatibility they carry, they report to the common sense as an embassy, until what is incompatible and what is compatible is presented to the rational soul (nafs natiqa). The soul then issues its commands for good and bad through the active faculty, and through knowledge it brings things into existence. Therefore, the address of reward and punishment cannot be directed to anything else. The agents carry out their functions, are established as such, and since human existence depends on this arrangement, it is maintained accordingly.

As has been mentioned, from the celestial spirit — which is the spirit of life and warmth — and from the elemental temperament, whose particular nature has been defined, and from the composition of the humors: sanguine, melancholic, bilious, and phlegmatic, it is compounded. From the beginning of creation, it is able to reach the form of the rank of the stomach, in that sense. And when it seeks nourishment and calls out, going through channels, it arrives at the rank of plant life, and from it springs a kind of movement and motivation, and from its pursuit of nutrition and nourishment, it reaches the level of animal existence, and its faculties take shape. And when over the rational soul and the universal soul, through His power, the intellect and speech are settled in their proper place — as is fitting — and the qualities and refinements are attained, and the rank of the body is completed for it, then the manners and disciplines of the highest order are acquired, and the noblest of creatures come to be known. As the poet says in a rubā'ī: "Go seek yourself — where are you? You are not outside yourself; look for knowledge within yourself." If you wish to know: the rational souls are luminous, free, and human in nature. Their existence comprises intrinsic virtues and moral qualities, descended from the spiritual world. Their aspiration rises above the animal world, and the body serves only as a vehicle for seeking the higher life. As God the Most High has said: "Those are like cattle — nay, they are even more astray," and "Most people are like cattle." All people other than the free, in their entirety, have been given the capacity for illumination, but in attaining the light of the goal, they fall short. As the poet Anwarī says in verse: "The one who has no fault does not err, even if he errs — it is still right." This is because a living body possesses particular qualities and human attributes. And the respected Shaykh Sa'dī — may God have mercy upon him — has said: eating is for the sake of living.

And you are certain that these worldly blessings will pass, and it is almost as if God has made you content. As for eating, do not be extravagant nor fall short — "neither be wasteful nor be miserly." The verse says: when weakness comes upon the soul, the Messenger of God said that Satan flows through the blood, and those who keep themselves hungry have been appointed as causes of harm.

One who eats little will not develop a bad character. For every morsel eaten, a hundred portions of provision are earned. And the Prophet said: "The stomach is the source of every illness, and abstinence is the foundation of every cure," and it was said: "The stomach is the seat of all disease." The physician who arrived and examined several patients said: however much you eat, your existence will persist in pleasure, your constitution will be sound, and your health will be maintained.

Someone said: Ibn Qadam al-Khubz said: "This amount is impossible, and more than this makes you pregnant with illness." Eagerness to eat and drink entirely corrupts and breaks one's character.

Know that one who submits to the appetite is lower than a slave to provision, and it is nothing but a carcass upon which dogs fight over. From among those who eat much, gluttony is produced. It was narrated: "The world is a carcass, and those who seek it are dogs."

In verse: The world is like a dung heap, and the ravens and vultures number in the thousands. Among the ignorant who are drawn to it — and among those who are bound by gold and silver, who are carried upon it — beware of staying behind. Striving and toiling for its accumulation leads nowhere.

The sum of all this: its blameworthy quality is that whoever gathers it for its own sake will find that the Messenger of God said: "Do not accumulate wealth" — for it leads to meanness of character, childishness, and boasting.

Dominant greed, severing family ties, preferring this world over the next, and striving for worldly gain — these are the qualities of the mouse and the ant. Being excessively eager like cattle, and donkeys, and being miserly — these are qualities of ignorance. Abu Jahl's quality is to gather everything whose meaning is only to squander it, and to seek only pleasure.

Fleeing from Satan, the rejected one, I seek refuge in God from these vile and base qualities.
Even though the essence of the newly-born soul turns toward the physical world and becomes aware of the world of elevation,
nourishing the mind with abundant knowledge — "None remember except those of understanding" —
its condition became clear, and the subtleties of realities and the arrangements of the decrees of creation were set upon the heart.
The wonders of the Maker's crafts and the verification of the Creator's unity became manifest — as is fitting,
so that the conscience becomes truly established and demonstrated: "Were the veil lifted, my certainty would only increase."
An angel arrives, as the Arabic saying goes: "We sought understanding, seeking nearness to God."
Following this path, connected and united, the servant finds no refuge except in God — hence all
words and the completion of messages occurred, making manifest what was hidden — "How excellent!"
"I knew creation so that I might know myself" — this is the meaning of "I would not have created the spheres."
In the form of the unity of the blessed existence — "Peace and blessings of God be upon Muhammad and all his companions" —
the culmination of creation was attained, and the ultimate meaning in the world was revealed.
We undertake with four perspectives, with God's help and His grace, the explanation of the nature of the human body's organs.
The second part: the explanation of the nature of the human organs,
understanding the composition of the form and meaning of the body's members and parts,
and the interplay and correspondence of fire, air, earth, and water elements,
and the garden of the soul in its spiritual refinement and nobility — may it be blessed —
attaining purity and nobility of the universal soul, praising the most elevated, gathering together in mercy,
in the smallest motion of the embryo lies proof of the power of the Maker and His wisdom —
praising God and the Divine — it is beyond reckoning that such a creation comes into being — what a wonder,
the first and the last, the two together, joined in permanence — and after truth comes the religion of completion.

In the self, the least of the celestial bodies — that is to say, from this account, the conviction and purpose
are such that the heart and inner self become receptive, and so it is said: "There is no god but God"
Praise be, the living and the dead, the dead and the living, and He gives life to whom He wills
The Master of all knowledge, and He is according to the measure of hearts, ascending unto Him in great exaltation, and so it has been since ancient times
It is correct that the members of the human body come into being through the four natural temperaments
And they are of two kinds: simple (mufradat) and compound (murakkabat), and in each there is a secret and a wisdom beyond reckoning
The intellect and understanding can hardly grasp the wisdom of their invention and the power behind their fashioning — it is beyond comprehension
And the tongue, as we said, was made receptive, for among all creation, only humans were addressed by the Most High
How is it that from nothingness, from non-existence, in an instant, He fashioned form — this is beyond any reckoning
Now it is noted that the simples (al-mufradat) are the simple organs, each having a subtle meaning
And their description comprises twelve properties. The bones (al-'izam) are cartilage that holds firm
The foundation of the body is built upon them, giving strength, so that the bones provide support and structure
They bring the muscles and skin close together, and provide the body's frame and support
For if the body's form were not proportionate, it would not be fitting, as the physicians of India have noted
The bones are the causes of all movements; if the bones were in several layers, the movement would become difficult
The organs of the body are connected through the bones, and they are joined together in proper arrangement
The purpose is to achieve suppleness of skin, and within it the bones — light and easy to move —
They should be light and easy to move, so that they desire nothing else, and God willing
The bones in certain places are harder, so that the marrow within them remains safe from harm
The moisture of the marrow reaches the bones and other organs continuously
The treasure within is internal and external, and the reason for this is the uprightness and goodness within and without.

A question: What do you see? The brain controls events, giving place and support, and in several ways it serves as the foundation. For the purpose of strengthening the limbs and nerves, and reaching the powerful members and extremities, and connecting to the bones, preventing injury to some, and certain ones do their work, establishing what is needed. It sits in place, and the sides, chest, hands and feet are given their arrangement. It accounts for the joints and the main articulations, and mentions for what purpose each member serves. The movement is weak in some, and the arrangement of the skeletal parts is composed of several layers. And the apparent movement belongs to the shoulder, hand, wrist, and the like. The bones interlock with one another, and are close to one another, moving at the ends. Fast-moving ones are called "free," and they move from that position. Those with no apparent movement, despite the presence of joints, are not like the head-turning and back-bending. And the teeth, and their like, among the joints, some are fixed. They sit in rows together, and the teeth close upon each other, and the bones meet at several points. Within the bones others fit together, and some stand upright, fused with one another, knit together. Those that were extended served the purpose of perfection of composition, and are named as such, giving rise to complaint. The total of the named bones, presented outwardly, is two hundred and forty-eight, in various shapes and descriptions as mentioned — located in places both large and small, moving and turning in different ways. The lower jaw is larger than the upper, serving chewing and speech, and there are eight of them. And the collarbone, the shoulder blade, the beak of the coracoid, the clavicle — all are named. The chest, the palm, the shoulder, the scapula, and the like — each in its proper place, arranged and measured, corresponding and connected.

The quarter-flat of the Salamiyans: the base of the jaw, the curve of the heel, the quarter-flat of the Salamiya.
The flank of the sa'l-'abd is described as surrounding the coccyx — the cartilage, so it is said.
It is called the "middle tendon" (habsi mutawassit); it is situated between the ligament and the bone, firmer than the ligament and softer than the bone. Its meaning is that it adds to the surface of the bone, resembling the type called sunntur.
From the knee it extends so that it comes between the motion of the hard bone and the soft flesh, so it causes no harm. The cartilage thus stands in the middle as an intermediary, and its meaning is that it replaces the separation of the bones through a composite structure, like flesh and fat, and what lies between the joints — if it were pure bone, the flesh would suffer immediate harm.
And if the flesh alone were bare, it would not accomplish the intended goal. The use of the cartilage is to prevent the bones from rubbing against one another, and from this comes the benefit.
The ligament (al-ribat) is the middle tendon (habsi mutawassit); it lies between the cartilage and is softer than the cartilage and harder than the tendon. Its nature is cold and moist. Its meaning is that in the joints of the bones it conveys the force of wet motion and prevents the warmth of motion from causing the bones to grind against one another and become damaged. It is mixed with nerves, and this is the cause of the moisture of all the organs, and it establishes their existence.
The habsi is soft and of the quality of hashim, and it has three qualities: the first is that it has good form but no motion; the second is that it has motion and good form; the third is that it has good form and also motion and good form together — this is the strong ligament.
It is intermediate between the ligament and the flesh, softer than the ligament. And if the flesh were hard, its nature being cold and dry, and it were dispersed — as it exists in the human body both inside and outside — then it would be possible for it to be both hard and soft, and the bones would remain fixed in their place; but great disorders

The existence of the human being is the most praiseworthy manifestation of the wisdom of the Creator, both in its outward and inward aspects. He has given the body nerves to convey sensations, so that the body holds together and nothing in the Creator's design goes awry. If any organ were to be disrupted, the nerves would lose their function, and reason and movement would be disturbed. Thus the hands, feet, neck, and their like, along with the nerves, sinews, and tendons, are held in balance. The nerves give strength and sensation, and through fear and other faculties they transmit signals, so that the intellect transmits commands from the brain to the limbs — this is the muscle. The nerves confine the soul within the body through anger and composure, keeping it in order, and thus the limbs perform their proper functions. When a muscle is in its place and the body moves correctly, the movement is smooth; otherwise there is disruption. Other muscles in other locations function differently, as has been noted: the muscles of the neck govern the head and neck; the muscles of the throat, jaw, cheek, chin, the skin of the belly govern swallowing; the muscles of the hand, fingers, and foot govern the upper and lower lip; the muscles of the leg and the bladder preserve urination; the muscles of the rectum preserve it; and all these nerves serve their appointed purposes. Flesh in general is soft and balanced, and it assists the nerves and tendons. If flesh were not there, the air would pass through the body directly, preventing digestion of food, and the passages would be blocked. Another benefit mentioned is that flesh keeps the shape of the body even and proportionate and gives it beauty and grace. Flesh is like red clothing upon the limbs — if a person of beauty becomes thin, that beauty diminishes and is harmed.

White meat is always good and gives freshness to the body; it increases beauty when eaten regularly. If people become thin, white meat is prescribed — it is not merely for purification or cleansing but for nourishment. Those who eat meat regularly and abundantly find that their body is well-nourished, and some transmitters and legal scholars report this as well.

The star (النجم): It is a pleasant, gentle creature whose nature warms the extremities like honey, and it is known among the names of things that have serpent-like qualities. It is among the first in the order of things that nourish the vital spirit. One of the greatest among them travels the path smoothly; it draws the animal spirit and maintains the breath.

It divides into small and great portions; the small ones come from the body cavities. The greater ones are reckoned among the treasures and maintain all the limbs with animal vitality, keeping the fresh ones vital. They nourish the body like a camel's sinews, and they convey the nourishment from the liver to all parts, distributing it through many branches from the interior. The liver's blood is thicker like settled earth, especially connected to the stomach; with warmth and moisture it helps digestion. If nourishment were not digested in the stomach, no organ would receive its proper share and all the body's parts would fail to obtain their benefit — and all bodily functions would be compromised.

Marginal note: Subtle, categorized.

Bring it, and it is like a fine layered garment, delicate and thin as gauze, acting as a repellent — for example, as it is said: it holds from grass, and among all these, the fine stars of Nazaki can enumerate and mention it. Since the remainder of the western ones are fine, temperate, and moderate in constitution, their arrangement inclines away from coarseness, being delicate and placed within the cavity of the bones in an organized fashion, bringing all together. It can reach the point of nourishment, being firm and strengthening, so that all levels can mention and attain it in time. Working from that, it moves and nourishes the interior. The Blessed Land is the friend of the soft belly, dark-complexioned, harmonious within itself, possessing natural firmness of body, and from its portions in proportion, keeping several among the unripe to full length, and bringing what belongs to it, pain and suffering from that. The flow and movement of that, being located in the sides of the limbs and wounds within: the internal voices are safe from afflictions, and the blows of grief and the great shadows become apparent. Glory be to Him who created the causes, and by His power the Compounds are apparent, as are the composite limbs. In their varied forms they encompass all, and in outward and inward qualities they are manifest. Let us name and mention the Head — the Head: since the outward senses, according to the scholars of the highest level, are necessary for the body, so that the senses may remain together in order and be capable, and the greatest movements may occur, He created it rounded so that when many wounds occur within it, it may also be resilient in many ways, and since it is rounded, it is less susceptible to harmful impressions, and may retain the best of forms. And He did not create it elongated so that all the nerves, as they come from the brain, and the bones of the skull — which all call firm and strong — may keep the wounds at bay, and the brain, hearing, sight, smell, and taste may all be under its protection. It was made several times over, maintaining strength for all, and each one like teeth...

Together they combine so that everything becomes one, complete in strength. Between the vertebrae and the marrow, a fine lining has been made from the outer layer so that it may be used purely. The marrow is conducted inward, and the external warmth of the body is kept away, so that its nature remains balanced. In the matter of the womb there is much variation, and for this there are many proofs. It is said that one could not travel to hell in a short time, nor hear it — though the ear trembles, one can hear it; hell cannot be seen from here. In truth, to summarize the meaning of the secret of the ebb and flow: the brain sends out fine nervous filaments throughout the body, as though carved, so that the body may be perceived in detail and functions are not lost — so that the brain need not travel great distances, and yet all the limbs may be reached. Fine nerves extend through the limbs, capable of bearing great length, running around the hard bones, conducting those fine nerves within — so that harms descending upon the body are resisted, no apparent disorder occurs, and hell is averted. Sometimes it protects from afflictions and keeps things sound, and at other times it endures blows so that damage does not increase. It multiplies and numbers them so that if one is injured, a hundred may suffer but another remains in place, and its owner is not entirely struck down and his vision does not fail. The finest and best of the body's members, like the movements of hand and foot — the body's nature can perceive and sense this, and the clear light works quickly and calmly so that one part serves another. The nerves from the brain to the body: some are brought to the utmost softness and fineness, and some are somewhat thick and firm, in proportion to their function.

He can introduce himself, and the origin of it, and the age, and the nerves from the back of the head reach the surface. Haytham considered the layers without distance, and the layers of Haytham, and its softness is harder than what is hidden. From the bier, the second layer can be perceived and upon it is a form like that of a horse's belly, and it is called the serous membrane, resembling a covering. He named it white and smooth, and he also called it the spinal covering. And from these layers, the fourth layer comes together like the sky of the fifth heavenly sphere. This layer he called the dense choroid, and the third, which is called the transparent, can be seen. And by mentioning both layers, they serve as protection from the harms of heat and cold, and they provide nourishment, and the fifth layer resembling this layer is like a spider's web, and the spider-web layer he named after it, and this is like the vitreous, and the sixth layer is white. Haytham called it the crystalline, it is black in appearance, and its surface is smooth. He called it the grape-like layer because it is shaped like a grape, half-formed, and has an opening in the seventh layer. In darkness it is wide, and in partial light it narrows, and the movement of the crystalline layer is for giving moisture, and the seventh layer he called it the outpouring. From it, fine moisture rains down and passes, and these seven layers, the sixth and seventh, are known for their clarity and luminosity, and the passage of nourishment between the two hollow nerves, from the front of the brain, the moisture that comes through the nerves and veins from the brain reaches the back, and quickly from the warmth, flowing one over the other, and those black moistures are given and pass.

When the body first comes into being through the womb, it is suited to receive and process the forces of armies that settle upon it — smoke, heat, cold, the storing of light and darkness and similar things — and it suffers from them. And in the wilderness it comes to itself and rises, and the upper part is the place of subtlety and great remembrance, while the lower part is settled and mountain-like, preventing and restraining. It is also called ghāzah. Just as night is a path that is traversable, so too the light of clear vision binds together what is near and joins two things, and the reason for the increase of its power is the EAR. The ear is like a spy within the body, and the king's secret agent, and for this reason it has the property of detecting, perceiving, hearing, and feeling. All that rises from the earth through the air comes to be known and is brought under control. The ear perceives it, and this nervous faculty carries the subtle perception to the brain. Within the inner chamber of the ear, the faculty of hearing resides, and the faculty of hearing with its form was given shape. If a veil comes between, deafness results, and the canal of the ear with its bone is called one of the greatest of things. The canal is smooth on the surface and the passage of marrow through it is complete, and [the organ] is strong. So that heat and cold and the blows of weather may not reach the hearing faculty, around it is something like a shell which resembles a conch. Its shape is like a shell, resembling curdled milk in form, and tiny hairs are set within it to bring sounds to their intended destination as perceived. And when the hearing is complete the purpose becomes known, and it is always slightly bitter. If the ear is harmed, the faculty of hearing is damaged. The NOSE: being well-proportioned in the face adds to the beauty of a person. And if the nose is of two [nostrils], the form allows the drawing in of air and the breathing out, giving access until the air becomes warm and heated, and this serves to warm and purify the air before it reaches the inner organ. And thus it renders the instrument perfect and pure. If the nose becomes overly moist through thick vapors or through excessive moisture, harm results therefrom.

The opening passage grants a benefit so that the inhalation becomes better regulated, and the passage of the pomegranate peel is brought forward. If harm comes to the acrid one, it remained in its place and the inner disturbance would not occur. He showed the path for those things — one part placed in the mouth with a pleasant fragrance of shanbī, and one part of pleasant nature for the throat, so that by exhaling through the nostrils, the air and scent are regulated, and the attracting moisture of the brain is treated. The air, according to what is established, and the balanced vapors are straightened, and it does not entangle with the king; both of these together remove malancholia, and these two together dispel heaviness of the brain. Like a crystal cup, it is drawn from the source of the spirits, and when it reaches the brain it is absorbed like a membrane. The brain and the vital spirit are attracted in the manner of pleasant medicines and the market of that path — the Senfar — the mouth recovers; by it the sense of smell and taste are revived and the teeth become able to chew food. Its nature is derived from firm meat and skin, and the nerves and muscles obtain from it movement, expansion, and contraction. And if it were more in the form of a complete human shape it would be harmful, and if its parts were of a nature to be separated, the excretions of its humors would be evident, and the benefit from it would have a proper reckoning. It was created from the forms of the embryo in order that the separation might come about and its benefit be obtained.

The Moon: In truth, the moon is not found in space as a void — it is something that passes, and since its existence is such that it passes, God Most High has said: "We have not made them bodies that eat no food" — so obtaining food for the upper world and for the purified body became necessary, and the provision of means was required. Just as it becomes obligatory — like the teeth for chewing food and swallowing, and the tongue for recognizing food and tasting —

The throat and larynx: the throat is used to keep food away from being inhaled, and to bring water down to the body; and just as nourishment is necessary for the preservation of existence, so too is breath, which draws cool air inward and expels warm air outward. The number of cartilages is said to be on the upper part of the body, and they are beside the throat. The vocal cords perform their function, and the throat acts as a passage; so that things pass through it and air moves freely in and out. The muscles cause the throat to dilate and contract, and breathing comes easily. In the area of the throat and toward the back of the mouth, for the purpose of drawing breath, the tongue acts like a small keeper that presses down so that the passage does not split open. At the time of eating and drinking, it signals so that nothing falls into the throat; and if, God forbid, something goes in the wrong way, it brings it back out. The throat for breathing remains open except at the time of eating and drinking, when its top is covered. And the reverse is true for the larynx — it too is closed except at the time of eating.

The tongue: the tongue moves with great speed, some say at seven thousand movements, and it refines a person's speech and is of service. It is made of white flesh mixed with nerves and vessels, and it receives sensation. It has two glands beneath it, in the form of sources of saliva, with two openings that keep the saliva flowing; and saliva moistens the food so that it may be swallowed. The tongue assists in tasting, speaking, and turning food around in the mouth. The tongue has two parts: one is apparent and the other is hidden beneath. If someone's tongue were to be cut and it were to break, harm and deficiency would result therefrom.

The section on Teeth: In the view of people of taste and discernment, the teeth are among the greatest works — they are like a necklace of pearls on the lips of the beautiful. Their appearance is like a witness of beauty, and the teeth are like brass in closeness to the gums and bones. Their substance is like tempered steel and iron, for the teeth are firmer and harder than the bones, their surface rougher and sharper, giving them their solidity. They are difficult to penetrate and resist being chewed through, and their hardness and roughness serve as a support. For the most part, the tissues around the teeth are firmly held in the flesh and bone so that with much movement they do not become loose; they stand side by side like soldiers in rank, each useful in its place, filling the gaps between them so that nothing can pass without their assistance, and they are indispensable to their function. The total number of teeth in each row is generally thirty-two: four incisors in front, called "quratum"; four beside them; four molars called "ansylt" and "fanus" (also called "istara"); twenty on one side and nineteen on the other — their number may exceed this. The section on the Sphere: The sphere moves by its nature seeking the celestial horizon, as the lower sphere moves according to the principles of anatomy, and its motion is like that of the higher sphere over the organs. This gives rise to spiritual motion; the lower sphere sustains the upper bones and the skull. It gives to every part in turn the same circular motion, and thus the result is recorded.

Regarding the description of the upper arm, forearm, and palm: it is the terminal part, and the bones of the wrist connect the palm and forearm, arranged side by side with the finger joints. The muscles and flesh are strong, and all the fingers together can form a grip, and from this grip and the motions of the tendons, actions are produced; the fingers can extend upward. With it one can benefit and repel blows; if the nail grows too quickly in the small finger, the captor of the nail preserves the inner tendon. It withstands shocks and, when strengthened, works like a screw.

From the beginning, movement is sustained for humans just as it is for animals, according to their nature. All together they are perfected, inclined toward uprightness and completeness. The Muslims in this rank, with devotion and obedience, bow in reverence — this is a sublime matter.

When it seems adequate, it can be drawn to the side with ease, and it comes, and so when Ibn Sughulta relates that the strength of the nerves prevents the nerves from the brain, and the brain cannot bear the burden of the nerves, divine wisdom has arranged it so that the nerves that go in and out are thick enough to travel the length of the body, so that the head is firmly supported, and the muscles, bones, veins, and flesh are as they should be.

The brain diffuses. The Heart — the heart is the sovereign and the essence of the body, like a king; it is the gathering of the pure spirit, the guardian of the spiritual and physical world.

The compound physical elements — meaning the simple elements — are the origin of the temperaments. The stable, strongest nourishment comes from the earth; from that, animal nourishment grows, and from the animal, the human is nourished. Just as from the human the limbs are formed and grow, so in the inner world, the soul of the human resides.

By perception and inner sight, intention is directed; one acts, and the Tradition of Unity is affirmed. As it is said: "My earth and My heaven do not contain Me, but the heart of the believer contains Me." And it is written: "He has inscribed faith in their hearts." The station is near, like two bow-lengths. Closeness and love are its highest degrees; the station of the world of the unseen names is the station of manifestation, the station of straightness and inwardness. Thus He has established Himself over the Throne — "The All-Merciful rose over the Throne" — meaning the heart is like the Throne: He bestowed His breath over it, for the Throne has no awareness and cannot ascend, while the heart of a human being is upright. If any human has such qualities, few possess them, and those are rare.

The noble Prophet, peace be upon him, has said in the Holy Quran: "In that there is a reminder." The heart that truly hears and sees — God Most High has said: "He came with a wholehearted heart." That is, the heart that comes into the presence of the Divine Majesty is truly present. Similarly, the outward form of the human being encompasses five senses on the outside; the heart likewise has five inner senses. The world of the unseen is not outside, but within — meaning it is the inward heart.

One who witnesses hidden matters and a child who is a listener to hidden speech will hear hidden things thereby and receive the taste of love, the sweetness of faith, and the desire for grace. And whoever keeps his senses sound and his mind intact, spiritual love will be realized in him and he will be among the saved; on the contrary, if his outward senses are impaired, no benefit at all will reach him. It was said: "The righteous person, when he performs righteous deeds, all his bodily members are well, and when he is corrupted, all his members are corrupted, and the heart is the most important — God Almighty made it so — and unless one comes to God with a sound heart, and the heart is kept pure and free of offense, the flow of the spirit's grace to the heart from the limbs will be cut off." All the limbs and organs are like caretakers, and if even one limb is rendered useless in its function and its power of contraction is lost, paralysis will affect it. Likewise, whenever a spiritual traveler turns away from the path of conduct and worship and abandons those practices, if he does not persevere patiently in those acts, his ruin will come and all his limbs will be laid waste. The heart resembles in shape a cypress tree — meaning it stands upright — and the spirit of animal life resides within it and spreads throughout the body, reaching the flesh and every part. There is yet another capacity: it guards against harmful things and is superior to the rational faculty. For this reason, the source of drink is the most delicate, the most refined, and the most sublime in degree. The reason is that the bones are the foundation and the deepest layer, containing hardness, and they preserve the body. Thus the body's existence remains, and the heart is cleansed and continually renewed, so that all other members are kept in order.

It settles in the heart and causes it grief and distress; it comes to the chambers on both sides. The ribs are the frame of the heart, which they call the foundation, and there are two of them. The hollows of the heart expand in their breadth and contract in their length. Since the heart is the source of the vital spirit and the sovereign of the body, its place is in the center of the chest. It is therefore necessary that the benefits and effusions flow easily to all the limbs and members. Since the foundations sustain it and protect it from external harm, it must be guarded so that the innate heat is preserved, and whatever reaches the organs and members is conveyed there. In the doctrine, the heart's position as sovereign of the body requires that it respond to all the limbs, and having done so, it carries out its functions without interruption. The body is sustained by its warmth, and by the nature and wisdom of the heart. It was therefore necessary that it be placed in the middle, equidistant from every side, so that the space within be ample and the digestion of food be easy. Each organ receives what is appropriate to it, and the wisdom of the heart, once understood, is that it exists and the heart governs the directions and guides the limbs and members. Behind and before, to right and left, it commands and situates the heart, and the wings and sides, before and behind, are arranged in the most excellent fashion, and the heart is established firmly. Among the subtleties is that it nurtures and warms what it receives. What remains flows through the channels, governed by the distributor, and the whole body is supplied. The vessels carry it further, flowing from the center of the chest to all sides. This is the vital channel, flowing from its source, and the sovereign power flows upward from the heart to the level of the limbs above the heart.

The greatest of the organs are the heart, for it is the source of the vital spirit; it is like an animal among the limbs, transmitting conditions both inward and outward, just as the brain translates and relays all the inner and outward states. If the brain's sensitivity is compromised, the qualities transmitted to it from the heart will be distorted, and the heart will likewise become disturbed. Cold and moisture descend from the brain, and by excess of these, the sensory faculties become impaired. Every sensation — love, fear, anger, grief, and joy — is transmitted so that the heart may be aware of all outward conditions and each faculty may become manifest.

It describes the composition of what is within, remedying it, and the amounts of what goes in and what it produces are all well-known and effective. It counts and enumerates the bones of the ribs and the joints, bringing them around, so that their number increases and they are controlled. It reports that the thickened and white fluid, like menstrual blood, flows in lines — sugar then carries what is appropriate out of the internal, and lapis lazuli is mentioned. Within, it causes descent by reason of the reproductive function, as has been said, and has not been read among those who have investigated it. For each of the parts of the back and other limbs, until the long space — it becomes wide, and at the time of expansion the urine flows and the semen comes out warmly. It is taken by the mountain, and of the caves it is pressed out, and it spreads and flows and the coarse and foolish things that are not sins, and fine things of the bones — and what is described is between the bladder and the rectum, and from those who are informed it is not difficult. Being lean and moist — the remedy comes down, pressing it out, and at the time of its exit, through the distance, it would not be seen.

The muscles of the womb become relaxed, and the eyes become dim, and the womb contains and holds the seed. The veins and vitality are set right, because the spirit from the heart arrives and the moisture diminishes. For this reason it is fitting and proper: the left side of the womb is opposite to this — it is fitting for [females]. The mouth of the womb and the membrane of the uterus at the time of delivery widen for the expulsion of the stone [i.e., the fetus], and the joint does not open too widely for men, until the reason reaches the fetus, and on the first day it proceeds. Thus the initial state pushes out the vapors and the subtle qualities of the fetus, and the moisture exhausts the membrane of the uterus — the humor dissolves from it and becomes thin — and the mind is disturbed, and it becomes receptive to the seed, so that until ejaculation by both the man and the woman, both seeds are destined for each other, and thus the seed settles on both sides. If the seed arrives with force and does not remain still, and the passage on the right side is also not passed through — the passage on the left side, however many layers of character it may have — then the question becomes dominant. And if the seed is stronger in quantity and does not pass through, then the passage will be that of a daughter. And if the passage is between the two — the mouth of the vagina — then, rarely in such a case, the form of a daughter will take on the qualities of a man, and it will mostly be so. The middle passage causes the seed to not pass through at all, and if by chance the seed does not pass to either side, it will be androgynous, and it will mostly carry the quality of both. The membrane of the uterus, when old, does not draw the seed into the womb. The number of children, because of the varied paths of the seed through the passages, is such that the ignorant do not know. The contraction of the womb afterward is proper, and the goat and the female, and the matter of circumcision, for the purpose of easing the pain — at the time of the seed's passage, man and woman and their mutual natural sensation are good-smelling, and [the body] gains a pleasing appearance, and the reason for the tongue's movement and its manner is like the passing of idhkhir [a fragrant grass].

On the failure to attain what is sought, with the excess of what is disliked and unwanted from creation — and the introduction and manners thereof — and in the fifth book: the coming together of the limbs and members of the human body.

Just as there has been mentioned of bones, cartilage, ligaments, muscles, nerves, and veins, and arteries, and the first cord, and fat, and flesh, and skin, and those things from the head — a great [number] of compositions has been enumerated, amounting to four thousand, which are said to be as the ancients have recorded.

The existence of the human being is sustained by branching connections that bind and reinforce, along with the nerves of the heart. And the speaking soul came to know, through the reality of knowledge and love, the unity of the Creator and the connection to it — reaching the utmost degree of longing and love, meaning the seeking of the Divine, which is the perfection of the human soul.

The people of the religious law, from among the prophets, have stated that God Most High has appointed over every human being twenty-four thousand guardian angels to protect and preserve his existence and to watch over him.

Know that God Most High said concerning this matter: "I brought him forth, and I cared for him" — and those who do not know this do not attain the stations of obedience and worship, which are the means of reaching and arriving at the ultimate goal.

And God Most High is exalted above any equal or helper. Worship and disobedience and opposition are decreed — not that God commands evil, but rather the performance of obedience and the avoidance of sin is incumbent upon those who are accountable before Him.

God Most High calls upon humanity to give thanks for His blessings, and to rise to gratitude, and to know His majesty and the glory of His unity.

The second attribute: on the mention of human pain — that God Most High placed within the human body, beginning from the face, various beneficial things in the chest, so that the humors of the body are set in order and the intended goal is attained. It is said that the gates [of the body] were opened and closed, and people busy themselves with worldly affairs while the city is adorned with beauty and ornament.

It existed, and in idleness one sleeps, for the sake of stillness the strong forces withdraw into the shelters; people are kept from work and livelihood, the city falls into decline.
The poet says: No season of birds, no pleasant air — the intimate companions of the masters are gone.

In the state of all the limbs and members of the human body, it is as if a well-furnished and adorned house, with its strong forces arranged like paintings and designs drawn in different colors throughout its chambers, so that when the steward of the house sets everything in order and arranges it well, those images and figures are kept in proper condition, and the weak are aided thereby.

The human soul, through its principal faculties of intellect, knowledge, and their like, secures and preserves all this. It is as if a lamp were lit within by reason of this meaning. And the meaning is this: by taking from those images and designs, a benefit results, and if the lamp sits still — that is, the soul performs its function of mediation — keeping all the conditions of the house in good order, the images arranged and the colors well-ordered throughout the house, they are of no use and no benefit.

Just as it has been stated: the human soul is a noble substance, not an accident; since its substance is transcendent and its existence is essential, not dependent on another's existence, and the lamp of the house likewise illuminates the interior. When one intends to depart, we say: do not go, for the judgment and command are not in your hands. Now, regarding this faculty in its description of exterior and interior:

The Exterior Faculties — these are touch, smell, sight, hearing, and taste — through which one comes to know the outward conditions of the world. The first of the senses is the most fundamental, shared by all animals; it is distributed throughout the body between the living beings, through the nerves from the brain throughout. From there something reaches and arrives, the covering of the fine membrane perceives it; information is cut off from the rest, and none of that is left unrecorded.

If the outer senses existed, the faculty of seeking nourishment from other than one's own parts would not be needed, and the sense of touch would be the least of them. It is therefore necessary that whatever is beneficial to existence should be recognized, and that this be perceived through the senses. The second point: sight requires a basis, since when something from the external world is present, guidance comes from it and the report reaches the mind.

The third point: vision needs a medium, for just as the inner faculties exist, so too must the outer ones, and it is necessary that the fourth sense, which is taste, also be present, so that by contact it may come to know what is beneficial, and what is proper to seek and obtain.

The fifth point: if all five senses were absent, the faculties that oppose harmful things would not function, and those inner faculties that God Almighty has placed in these outer senses and the faculty of the whole would deem the harmful acceptable and reject the beneficial, and wholesome nourishment, however present, would neither be consumed nor beneficial.

Thus the creature is raised from the rank of plant and animal to the rank of human, so that through it the gift of knowledge, the reality of the nature of the senses, and the quality of perception are bestowed. This quality is present in the skin of every being, so that through it warmth, coldness, roughness, softness, heaviness, tenderness, and the like are perceived.

The fifth sense, which is smell, brings pleasant and unpleasant odors to the brain, and the orderly nervous system distinguishes good from bad, and image from image. For if the visual power is within the eyelid, the reflection enters through the eye. If the visual power is spread throughout the body, the whole existence is filled. Whatever the eye perceives, the faculty reports it, and through the nervous system order is maintained, so that from all of these the inner faculties are sustained.

And in this way that [faculty] perceives it, for when the breath of the vital spirit rises to the place of the organ it will seek to draw the image of the air inward, and the vital spirit will be [present], and it will seek to take in the human impressions from without. The air necessarily goes inside and becomes a sphere, and it diminishes, and when the light of the auditory nerve enters, in the tympanic membrane of the ear the fluid is extended inward and perception occurs, and the faculty of hearing [receives] the impression. The sense of taste is located in the substance of the tongue, and its center is from the palate; its parts are combined together, and the tongue is blended and mixed, so it conveys [flavor] to those [centers] within. The pleasant and the sweet and the savory and those related to them, and the bitter and the salty — all are [present] in equilibrium. And through the strong and dominant faculties, causes of existence [arise] for the near and the evident, and it reaches [its goal], and it works from childhood, youth, and maturity onward. The inner faculty works through all the instruments, meeting [what comes to it], and the attracting force brings [the substance] with the intellectual [faculty] gathering it from all sides. And when that faculty acts, it has four qualities: first, the attracting [force], which draws from below, and it runs through every organ as a current flowing fast, and the blood attracting [nourishment] carries it to those parts. For example, when the nourishment sought by any organ exists, if another contrary organ is present, with its conditions of moisture, warmth, sweetness, pleasantness, bitterness, saltiness, and the rest — each element keeps its own quality in twos, and the taste of each compound draws [its part] down within. Then whenever [an organ] has something beyond [its need], it gives back the surplus without benefit, and the blood the attracting [force] mixes together.

For months it restrains and controls, keeping the nourishment in place; and so it expels from the organs what is suitable, and whatever of the surplus nourishment is not needed by those organs, it expels it, just as nourishment suitable for an organ increases by the removal of waste from it.

Then likewise there are four stages: the beginning, the rise, the [peak], and the decline. The organ draws the nourishment to itself, and whatever is surplus to the organ's needs passes on to other organs, so that nothing is wasted and the proper amount remains. Each organ receives according to the proportion suited to its nature, and what is not consumed by that organ is passed on, and the remainder provides nourishment appropriate to it and sustains it.

Sometimes the nourishing power is in excess, sometimes deficient, and sometimes balanced, and the sustaining power in the organ remains constant. If it is excessive, waste products are produced, and one can observe this in animals, plants, and minerals throughout the world.

The forms thus take various shapes according to what is appropriate for each: long, short, round, flat, thick, thin, coarse, or fine. And the benefits thereof are that when nourishment passes through its own channels to the limbs and organs of animals, one can observe the wisdom of God the Exalted.

The attractive faculty draws forth the food sought by the organism and delivers it through the digestive process to all the limbs and organs. The retentive faculty draws the nourishment in and holds it; the nutritive faculty maintains the organ in its proper state, being the cause of the organ's subsistence.

The formative power shapes the blood into various forms such as bone, flesh, sinew, and so on, which are then transferred and transformed, replacing what has been consumed, just as is observed.

One must observe the proper proportions of forms according to need and necessity, and similarly one must not neglect them, for if a limb were to come from this form, and the substance of every limb were perfected, then the share of each one would be proportional to what it was, and the form would rise up accordingly — and the shape that was hidden within it would become apparent, and the share of each limb would require due consideration.

Thus one does not err in understanding the body and its coarseness, and its like is thereby attained, without deflection or deviation from the proper measure. Every individual among the common people is necessarily suited to be accepted by wisdom, so that what is born may prosper, and the remnants of the body's parts may be made easy, and reproduction may be facilitated, so that the survival of the human species may be ensured.

The Painter of forms looked upon it, so that in the inner darkness He drew most beautifully the parts and members — one more wondrous than the next — each organ aiding the other, and each assisting what comes after it. He then looked upon the mystery of the parents and what they produce, so that the interior and exterior of the embryo could be witnessed and observed.

How then could one not glorify the Maker and Creator, and sanctify and praise Him? In all the atoms of this great world, the hearts of those who are spiritually deaf and blind — even if they witnessed it — could not truly understand the nature of His might and glory.

The mark of the third faculty — the cognitive imagination — is this: it retains the images of perceived things after perception ceases. The first group, the special ones, is such that among them, sensory perceptions remain as witness. One must, by way of investigation, distinguish between pure beauty and shared beauty — for those of lesser capacity can perceive shared beauty together and see it, but pure beauty they cannot fully investigate or realize, and the faculty of imagination remains...

In the middle of the brain, holding the position of a treasury, is the common sense faculty. The common sense perceives it; imagination is rarely found settled there, and it is established within the brain. It processes and composes the forms that exist in imagination. As for the faculty of meanings, it works alongside imagination — if it accords with reason it is called compliant, if it opposes reason it is called fanciful — and the imaginings that are irrational. The posterior part of the brain is the storehouse of memory. That is the nerve of retention, and the three sensory nerves belong to it — they are the faculty of smell, and the force of cold is also attributed to it.

It numbers a hundred thousand, and among them those who have devoted themselves to asceticism number a hundred thousand, and among those who travel in Khorasan who long for food — if they are not voluntary in their faculty — they seek food and then stop; the reason for this return and stagnation is that if this type were not prevented, the bodily parts would diminish, the strength would weaken, and the humors would be disrupted. Just as illness — however slight its cause — brings about the loss of appetite, so too does this arise.

Such are among the special properties of the body. By the wisdom embedded in the animal nature, when appetite is lost, the faculty ceases, and the animal's nutrition is suspended, and since it is necessary for it to cease, it no longer seeks food; and the limbs and organs return to their own qualities and characteristics. The second type among the group is the transferring kind — that type whose action is such that of that type the intermittent cuts off, and from the transferring it draws away.

The existence and non-existence of a seeker becomes established, and the capacity for intellectual power remains, and the power of reason prevails. If it overcomes something, it does so for the sake of attracting benefit and repelling harm, and in all inner faculties it is present, and in other animals it is abundant — that is, fleeing from harm toward benefit. Except in the evil eye, which is hidden; it is as though it is established in the nature of creatures. The evil eye operates in both the one present and the one absent, from a certain direction — meaning the evil eye is something that strikes and settles in the middle of the brain. It perceives the sensible things and imagines them, and honesty in it binds enmity between enemies, and from this foundation the nature is formed. Its benefit at the appropriate time is a lasting achievement, for from the occurrence of what is produced — through contraction, expansion, nourishment, and relaxation — the nerves are strengthened. And at this time in animals it leads toward requesting and seeking. The seeker is made to hear and is freed from cunning, and it has four divisions.

First: among horses, among middle animals, and among other creatures, they are prepared for theoretical, reflective, and practical knowledge. Second: in human beings — children and adults — they are not merely potential, but actually present. It is not mere habit. It is called the royal intellect, and it pertains to the faculties of the senses and their domains. Just as when one calls out to someone wonderful, it becomes obligatory to command, forbid, and distinguish the army — knowing that a person is a human being, and not an animal, and so forth. From the royal intellect, the faculties of the senses and the power of attainment do not record in the mind, but the strength of comprehension is obtained through experience, and the wise person's intellect is held in esteem. It investigates the state of affairs and manages matters accordingly. One who hastens toward immediate pleasures and does not grasp ultimate ones loses them — and so too is the intellect.

By the intellect come benefits and the refinement of human minds. The lover of noble intellects, from the beginning of the age of discernment until the age when ignorance holds sway — which is the limit of the perfection of the intellect — is the self.
The denial of this meaning is impossible, since it is observable that some go along with it, and in resolving subtle questions they proceed swiftly. The expression indicates honor, and the inward signs of the heart become clear, and the dull-witted [remain] as they are, instructed.
Among them some are counted, and they reckon them thus; and the proof of prophecy becomes manifest in the refinement of intellect. It is as if Ibn Sallam narrates it at the end of a long hadith:
In the description of the Throne, it is said the angels said: "O Lord, have you created anything from the Throne?" He said: "Yes, the Intellect." They said: "What is its extent?" He said: "Far be it! How can you reckon this?" A servant of humble station asked: "Is there none?" He said: "No." He said: "Then I created the Intellect in types and divided it among people: among them some were given one portion, among them some were given two portions, and among them a third, a fourth, and among them some were given six portions of that — glory be to Him — and the benefit reaches all friends, rather all people, so that each one has a sufficient share of reason, as has been stated."

The Third Quality: On Mentioning the Special Properties and the Creation of Limbs and Organs
All animals, including humans, in relation to them — as for the special properties, which are claimed to be specific — these thirteen: the first is the absolute and primary quality of humans among all beings.
And the power that humans possess exceeds that of other animals, and indeed God has honored the children of Adam: He made him upright in stature, capable of speech, unlike other animals who bend down to the earth.
He wishes to make the uninitiated understand, and by signs and gestures conveys meaning to those who do not understand. And if the listener is slow in comprehension, he considers it until insight and reflection arrive.
The second: it is revealed through contemplation that the hidden becomes uncovered and manifested. The third: likewise.

On the subject of hair: it was created on the head of the human being for beauty and adornment, also serving to protect the brain and body from harm. The body benefits from it, for it draws out fine superfluities through fine pores in a refined manner. Hair was placed on the top of the head where it serves as an ornament and also repels certain harms from the person. Hair is related in the common tongue to warmth, and the strange heat that cooks the humors causes it to grow; and the whole purpose of showing these members is that moisture must necessarily diminish within the body. When the natural faculty is insufficient, the body of necessity produces this growth. When someone has an organ affected and sees children, the arousal intensifies. If a large number of men gather and one of them looks upon the others with desire, the owner himself is also affected. Bathing in a bathhouse with someone who has mange causes contagion; if one sits in the same session one passes it to the other, and if one walks barefoot on the ground where a person with leprosy has walked and the soles of the feet and body touch it, the infection spreads. Concerning young girls at the age of seven: if a eunuch arouses them they will stir and react. As for asafoetida: if someone smells it and desires its taste, their blood becomes like that of a weakened person, and their limbs become feeble. Likewise, a person who digests poorly becomes weak and feeble, their limbs grow slack, their desire for food diminishes and their appetite wanes; but their desire for intercourse grows stronger and their lust increases. For this reason excess moisture causes the limbs to swell and weakness results.

From this one can understand that the special property and affinity of the humble and the refined,
And the auditory pleasures increase, and one becomes quick to anger and quick to be pleased, and the gaze soothes,
Comprising the power of sexual union, and if it be with a virgin, it causes harm,
And the loss of potency has been noted in this connection, so that the duration diminishes,
More than others, for those who are considered wise, because of strong constitution,
From among those who remain capable and strong in their active state, and especially
When a woman exposes herself and is available, its flow is cut off, and if it spreads further,
And applied to the head and between the shoulders, and if rubbed between the shoulders, it is absorbed,
And blood from wild beasts, if administered internally, shows its effect through untamed nature,
Others have also noted that when applied to the joints it stops the burning pain, and if used
At the time of paroxysm, the aloe mixed with bitterness acts as a remedy, and remedies are found in its approach,
It becomes turbid, and if used by an epileptic or one touched in the mind, it relieves the back pain, and as a remedy,
And if pomegranate and sheep's fat are used, rubbing the sheep repeatedly because of the belly and digestive complaints,
It returns, and if applied with pressure, binding with winds opposing and alien,
For a menstruating woman, after washing, if the one in need is given it, it becomes acceptable,
The eleventh: if a man enters into relations with a woman while she is in a high state, and penetration occurs, the freshness and moisture remain,
And the treatment is done, and by the truth of the matter the foolishness becomes clear, and the Jews
Consider such relations with the descendants as reading, and call it madness, and consider it forbidden, and it is whispered about.

And others such as Thurayba did not create, and Kusayld, the great ones likewise perished, and the seventeenth, the models —
especially through the intermediary of moisture and material, a great deal was obtained, and the people came to know
and from this poison, it is not human that it issued from them, and their limbs could not [bear it] —
because the animal does not reach: First observation — the benefits of the limbs and the running of the human body are
from these things, let us mention: first, that human hair, when boiled, the owners
put it in water mixed with it, ground it up, and the head of a human, having been buried with juniper —
bury it, and black doves will gather there, and in it a lofty benefit will be found,
from that place, the second: if the one afflicted with the stone illness recites and reads —
the skull of a human for three days with little honey, and warms it — it will benefit;
the bone of a dead man placed on one who has quartan fever will stop the fever and return to ashes —
if an epileptic takes some of it to Safa in Babel — the brain of a human, foremost, applied on pomegranate skin —
with coriander and other insects, ground finely, blown inward, will drive out [the affliction], and will send four messengers to the person —
when in a state of excitement, mixed with cold water, like a fine example — in a narrow vessel —
and if the epileptic drinks pressed [juice], and on the contrary, will strengthen and make them firm —
the great and mighty will hear it, and it will come, as if the water of its name is brought forward —
the wonders of the disagreements will be spoken of, claiming, and those thought to be mad from scorpion [sting] —
will be helped; ebony wood, kohl of antimony, camphor, myrrh —
rub it with water of the mouth of a person and bring water of the mouth to a magnet —
the mouth pains will stop, and the first teeth, knock them loose —
throw them on the ground thus; if for a Solomon it comes, Providence will make it easy —
it will be heard, and rubbing the teeth of a dead man on [living] teeth — in the inner part it will stop the pain.

If a turtle is born under the wind sign and reaches Egypt, with its shell on its back, it will not be harmed.
If one of its claws is placed under the little finger as a talisman bearing the name Ptolemy, it will bring safety.
[A preparation] ground fine with a stone, given to the owner of the name, will bring purification and remove excess.
Whoever is not aware of this: take the fingernail, place it among old things, grind it fine with human blood — it will work.
Place it among the grasshoppers so that they settle and leave the land without harm, and the people's blood will not flow — it will work as a protection.
This blood, if applied, and if a mad dog's saliva is added, will bring healing.
It benefits against vitiligo and leprosy, and is useful for many ailments.
Apply it, ground, with the virginal matter of a pure white girl — pour it on.
Place it on a girl who has not yet known a man; it will settle and take effect.
If someone anoints himself with this, vitiligo and skin conditions will be alleviated.
If the preparation is made and applied, it will cause hair to grow on bald spots, and if water is added to it, it will also work.
Dry this preparation, give it to a woman to smell — her menstruation will cease.
The twelfth: the veins of a person, when collected and combined, will produce [a remedy]. The loss will be reduced and the vessels will work well.
Apply it with coriander water and it will adhere well.
The thirteenth: the tongue, with honey of the jujube, used for bladder and urinary complaints — take it and add saffron mixed with it, and it will settle the inhabitant.
The fourteenth: human perspiration, boiled with orris root — it will settle urinary disturbance, calm nocturnal emission and related complaints.

They boil it in a copper vessel with honey; it removes white discharge and similarly, when given to a person suffering from jaundice so that he does not know what to eat, it is eliminated in the manner described by Paulus. The urine of a person who had a skin ailment on his back is removed; the owner of the ailment recovers. And if there is mange with itching, prepare the female compound. In the hidden properties it has come: give it as a drink to the owner of a spleen ailment for two or three days until his urine clears, so he is freed; give it to him along with all foods not eaten raw. Give it to make a blind person see; it removes the veil from his sight and allows him to recognize people. If applied to mange, it heals; it removes the itching from those nearby and in extreme cases it tightens the abdomen. With white antimony it removes discharge and is extremely beneficial.

Second Consideration: On the Ethics/Nature of the Almighty — exalted be His glory — and the matter of angelic and sovereign qualities: They are endowed with beautiful traits and are patient, they are coupled together, and the Shia say: "God created the angels from intellect without passion, and created the beasts from passion without intellect, and created mankind from both — whoever's intellect dominates his passion is better than the angels, and whoever's passion dominates his intellect is lower than the beasts." In every individual both qualities exist. But the wonder is that the capacity of the rational soul varies, and likewise among all creatures there is variation, proportionate to the human being. And the poets say — and how many are the differences among men, like a hundred to one — and in the rarities of wonders: this is because in man these qualities exist to the utmost degree. Some say that for the refinement of good qualities, if in reality these qualities return to decline, they will not remain, and if they overcome the decline and reach the rank of angels, they purify the soul toward the angelic.
